content.prompt:
Find the volume of this square pyramid. Answer to 1 d.p.

(Hint: you are given the edge height; to make a right-angled triangle you need to use the diagonal of the base.)

spec.description: Square pyramid with four equally marked base sides. Rear base boundaries and the rear apex edge are dashed; silhouettes and visible edges are solid. The 25 cm label belongs to an apex-to-base-vertex edge.
spec.mathematics: Square base side 20 cm; sloping edge 25 cm. The perpendicular height is not supplied.

answer.worked:
Let $d$ be the base diagonal and $h$ the perpendicular height.

$$\begin{align*}d&=\sqrt{20^2+20^2}=20\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\\h&=\sqrt{25^2-(10\sqrt{2})^2}\\h&=\sqrt{425}=5\sqrt{17}\text{ cm}\\V&=\frac{1}{3}Ah\\V&=\frac{1}{3}(20\times20)(5\sqrt{17})\\V&\approx2748.7\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.method: Find perpendicular height using Pythagoras without rounding, then apply V = Ah/3.

content.prompt:
A triangular pyramid has a base with sides 16 m, 17 m and 17 m.
The height of the pyramid is 20 m. What is the volume of the triangular pyramid?

(Hint: you need to use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the height of the base triangle)

spec.description: Triangular pyramid with a hidden rear base edge labelled 16 m by a leader. Matching ticks identify the two 17 m base sides. A separate leader labels the dashed perpendicular pyramid height 20 m; its foot has a right-angle cue.
spec.mathematics: Isosceles triangular base with sides 16 m, 17 m and 17 m; perpendicular pyramid height 20 m.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied dimensions and equality marks are visible; the base-triangle height is not supplied.

answer.worked:
The height of the isosceles base triangle bisects its 16 m side.

$$\begin{align*}h_{\text{base}}&=\sqrt{17^2-8^2}\\h_{\text{base}}&=15\text{ m}\\A&=\frac{1}{2}\times16\times15=120\text{ m}^2\\V&=\frac{1}{3}Ah\\V&=\frac{1}{3}\times120\times20\\V&=800\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.method: Use Pythagoras for the necessary perpendicular height, retain exact arithmetic, then apply V = Ah/3.

content.prompt:
Archimedes also found that, for a sphere that fits perfectly inside a cylinder:
$$\frac{V_{\text{cylinder}}}{V_{\text{sphere}}}=\frac{SA_{\text{cylinder}}}{SA_{\text{sphere}}}$$
Show that this is true.

spec.sourceRegion: Lower question, left-hand sphere in cylinder
spec.description: Unshaded sphere inscribed in a cylinder, with solid silhouettes and a dashed hidden rear bottom rim. Source blue outlines become ordinary black geometry.
spec.mathematics: Sphere and cylinder share radius r; cylinder height is 2r.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied fitting relationship only; no dimensions or derived ratios are added.

answer.short: Both ratios equal $\frac{3}{2}$, using the cylinder's total surface area.
answer.worked:
Let the common radius be $r$. The cylinder's height is $2r$.
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{cylinder}}&=\pi r^2(2r)=2\pi r^3\\V_{\text{sphere}}&=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\\\frac{V_{\text{cylinder}}}{V_{\text{sphere}}}&=\frac{2\pi r^3}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}=\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$
Using total surface area, including both circular ends:
$$\begin{align*}SA_{\text{cylinder}}&=2\pi r^2+2\pi r(2r)=6\pi r^2\\SA_{\text{sphere}}&=4\pi r^2\\\frac{SA_{\text{cylinder}}}{SA_{\text{sphere}}}&=\frac{6\pi r^2}{4\pi r^2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{align*}$$
Therefore the volume ratio equals the surface-area ratio.
